name: Predictive Coding and Technology-Assisted Review
title: Predictive Coding and Technology-Assisted Review
answer: Predictive coding and technology-assisted review, often called TAR, are methods for finding relevant documents in large collections during discovery, investigations, and regulatory responses. They use a human reviewer's judgments on a sample of documents to train a system that ranks or classifies the rest. The scope covers email, chat, contracts, and other unstructured text, often in matters with hundreds of thousands or millions of files. TAR is used to reduce manual review cost and time while aiming for defensible recall of responsive material.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Predictive coding and technology-assisted review, often called TAR, are methods for finding relevant documents in large collections during discovery, investigations, and regulatory responses. They use a human reviewer's judgments on a sample of documents to train a system that ranks or classifies the rest. The scope covers email, chat, contracts, and other unstructured text, often in matters with hundreds of thousands or millions of files. TAR is used to reduce manual review cost and time while aiming for defensible recall of responsive material.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on standard e-discovery platforms that store processed text and metadata in searchable indexes. Training and ranking typically happen on cloud or on-premises servers with enough memory to hold document vectors or term weights for the collection. No specialized hardware is required for most matters, though very large corpora may use distributed processing. The system needs access to the same extracted text, metadata, and family relationships that reviewers see.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: A senior reviewer codes a seed set or iterative samples of documents as responsive or not responsive. The software learns from those labels and scores the remaining population, often using logistic regression, support vector machines, or similar text classifiers. Reviewers then examine high-scoring documents, and the process repeats until the rate of new responsive material falls below an agreed threshold. Quality is checked with control sets and statistical sampling rather than by reading every document.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Courts and parties generally accept TAR when the process is transparent, documented, and validated. Key risks include inconsistent training labels, hidden custodians or date ranges, and over-reliance on a single model without measuring recall. Parties often negotiate a protocol covering seed selection, confidence levels, and disclosure of non-responsive documents. The defensibility rests on showing a reasonable, repeatable method rather than a perfect result.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: TAR is moving toward continuous active learning with smaller initial samples and earlier quality control. Generative models are being tested for summarization, privilege review, and first-pass issue coding, but human validation remains central. The next few years are likely to bring more integration between TAR and large language models for concept-level review, with courts still focused on measurable recall and process transparency.
